messages.body_plain:
Hi All --

I'm working on analyzing some point count surveys (in this case of primates
-- I realize that usually line transects are used for primates, but this
particular area is quite mountainous and thus straight line transects are
really, really hard to set up). We have 118 point transects at three
different areas, with coverage of 4 habitat types, point transects were
established more or less at random with regard to primate locations
(actually they were set up for a bird survey). For each of 3 species we
have 110-280 observations per species, with distance from center of point
to center of closer, and cluster size. Data were collected by local
observers -- they received training but are not scientists, and this is
affecting the data. The closest observations are on the points, the
farthest are about 80 m from points (forested area) but the number of
observations drops off a lot after 50 m.

I am having a couple of questions -- I have tried searching and while I
suspect they are common, I wasn't able to find a satisfactory answer
(perhaps I am not using the correct terminology). If you now of an earlier
message that addresses these issues, I would be grateful for someone to
point me towards it.

The first problem I am having is with rounding of data. Although we ask
observers to measure distances, there is a clear tendency to round to the
nearest 5 m (e.g., lots of observations around 25m or 30m, but way fewer at
27 or 28 meters). We will address this in future work, but in the meantime
I am looking to analyze the data in intervals to deal with the heaping. But
I am unclear on *how* to decide what intervals to use -- I know I want them
to be away from where the heaping is, but aside from that, is it simply a
matter of trying lots of different combinations of intervals (lots of small
intervals? fewer larger intervals?) and seeing which ones give the best
model fit? I imagine this is a frequent question but my searches did not
turn up the depth of information in the answer I'd hoped for -- I would
greatly appreciate anyone pointing me in the direction of a good reference
for the process.

Additionally, there are some point transects at which primates were never
observed. Mainly this is because these points happened to be in a habitat
type the monkeys will occasionally enter, but do not favor. (I am
stratifying the analyses by habitat type.) I am unsure of how to deal with
survey effort there -- do I include a record for that transect point and
they survey effort, but then leave the distance and cluster size and
species blank? Obviously I want to include that survey effort in the
analysis so as to not artificially inflate density estimates, but am not
quite sure how to include that in the data table.

Thanks

Kim

kimwil...@gmail.com

messages.body_plain:
Kim:

A couple of thoughts about heaping taken from various list-server=20
comments (performing a search on the term 'heaping':

11 Sept 2011 Prof. Buckland

if you rely on chi-sq gof, you need to choose cutpoints well away from fa=
voured
rounding distances. If you do, you shouldn't see that level of sensitivit=
y. Without careful choice
of cut-points, gof isn't very useful if you have heaping. It's not tellin=
g you about model
mis-fit - just that you have a problem with the data.

 From 29 July 2004 Prof. Buckland

> > How does one decide what the best grouping is to reduce the effects of =
heaping?
  I can't seem to find a definitive answer in the manual/book.

I would not choose intervals with reference to goodness-of-fit statistics
- though a good choice of groups should improve the reliability of gof
tests.  I would examine the data, and the behaviour of my observers, to
determine what the favoured rounding distances are.  I would then choose
cutpoints to try to ensure that these favoured distances fall well away
from cutpoints.  In this way, few observations should end up in the wrong
group.

18 Mar 2004 Jeff Laake

Data collection process and accuracy of your measurements should guide
your binning choice and not the cv of density.

See also the following sections of Buckland et al. (2001):
2.1.3.1
4.5 "If values tend to be recorded to the nearest 10m, cutpoints might=20
be defined at 5, 15, 25m,..."
5.5 (heaping and point transects)

General guidance on heaping is to not use trial and error, but rather=20
try to understand the magnitude of measurement error and do your best to=20
select interval cutpoints such that the actual distance falls within the=20
proper bin.

Regarding data entry for points without detections you are exactly=20
right:  record the visit and the effort expended, but the fields for=20
sighting distance and group size are blank (most definitely do not place=20
'0' for sighting distance which implies there was a sighting exactly on=20
the point).

Hope that is useful.

messages.subject: Question about dsm 2.0 in combination with MRDS analysis
messages.subject_clean: Question about dsm 2.0 in combination with MRDS analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hello dear listees! We are working on a dsm analysis of a double observer
ship survey using dsm 2.0 in R. So far, we have our dsm model up and
running using an MCDS detection function with one 3 level factor. We also
have an MRDS running in R (mrds 1.5, I believe... the newest one from CRAN)
as well as in Distance 6.0r2 (with built in mrds and dsm package).
Thankfully, the MRDS and MCDS in both approaches yield similar results. We
would like to know how we can incorporate the findings of the MRDS into our
dsm detection model, since in a conventional MCDS setup, the p0 (and thus
the corrected one derived from the MRDS) should basically be treated as the
proportion of animals seen / missed and should thus be used as a correction
factor to our abundance and density estimates. However, in a dsm
environment, we are not sure if that approach is applicable, since the
detection function is used to produce 'local' estimates of abundance and
thus of density, which are then estimated for the whole of the study area
by summing up the individual cells (which are, by the way, regular squares
of fixed width and height). If we have a p0 for the detection function of
lets say 0.62, does it translate directly to "whatever the result of our
dsm using that mcds model was, it is about 40% too low"?

Another, quite unrelated question:

I am wondering a little about the Density estimates produced by dsm 2.0.
While abundance estimates seem to be reasonable and even give reasonable
cv's in both the variance propagation approach and the generic approach (no
bootstrapping), density estimates seem to be a little high (but still
feasible), while the associated estimated cv's of the density estimates are
waaaaaay off (1000 % CV???) How come? Shouldn't we excpect a density
estimate close to total abundance divided by total grid area? And thus a
similar cv distribution as for the abundance estimate?

PS: Our data does not seem appropriate enough for the dsm supplied with
Distance 6.0r2 and there is no hope of convincing it to be kind to us, so
we'll have to stick to the dsm 2.0 in R (on a side note, it is also fast as
lightning...)

Thanks in advance!

--
